plain_summary: The Mravic lab designs artificial proteins that insert into cell membranes, a notoriously difficult environment to engineer because membranes are greasy and proteins there often misfold or resist study. Using computer-based ("de novo") protein design, the lab builds synthetic helices that interact with natural membrane proteins—ion channels, immune receptors, and hormone receptors—to stabilize them, block them, or control their signaling. They also build laboratory tools to measure these membrane interactions inside living human cells, and use computer simulations to understand how molecules like antibodies dock onto membrane surfaces. This work matters because many drugs target membrane proteins, and misfolded membrane proteins cause disease; being able to design custom molecules that bind and control them opens new paths toward therapeutics, disease-correcting "chaperones," and new tools for structural biology.
trajectory: Early work (2021) established basic design principles, building water-soluble helical barrels convertible into ion channels and using microfluidic screens to probe signaling domain coupling. More recent papers (2023-2026) shift toward therapeutically relevant applications: designing transmembrane proteins that bind and regulate specific human receptors (EpoR, TLR4), developing high-throughput human-cell assay platforms (MemPPI) for membrane protein-protein interactions, and creating accessory subunits that stabilize disease-relevant membrane proteins. The trajectory points toward de novo transmembrane protein design as a general platform for engineering receptor signaling and building molecular tools and therapeutic leads for membrane protein targets.
